codes.title: Drop the sorry
lines: Most apologies in conversation aren't apologies. They're permission requests: is it okay that I'm talking?
Every unneeded sorry tells the listener to take what follows less seriously. Two in a minute and they will.
Keep the real ones: you bumped someone, you were late, you hurt them. Cut the rest.
Replace 'Sorry, quick question' with 'Quick question.' Replace 'Sorry, that was rambly' with nothing. Just stop and let them talk.
Drill: one conversation today where you notice the urge and say the next sentence instead.

codes.title: Say the specific thing
lines: 'I work in tech' ends a conversation. 'I build the thing that flags fake reviews on Amazon' starts one.
The specific version feels riskier because it can be judged. That's exactly why it's interesting.
When someone asks what you do, what you're into, or how your week was, find the one concrete detail and lead with it.
Then stop. Let them ask. The follow-up question is the reward.

codes.title: Entering a group that's already talking
lines: Don't interrupt and don't hover. Stand at the edge, catch the eye of whoever's talking, and listen for ten seconds.
Your first contribution should be about what they're discussing, not about you. A question or a reaction.
Introduce yourself in the first natural pause, briefly. Name and one hook.
Rooms forgive late arrivals who add to the conversation. They punish ones who reset it.

codes.title: The pause is not your enemy
lines: A one-second pause before a hard answer reads as thought. A filler reads as panic.
When you feel the 'um' coming, close your mouth and breathe through your nose. Then speak.
The silence feels ten times longer to you than to them.
End sentences on a full stop and let the air sit. People lean in to silence.

codes.title: Saying no without the essay
lines: The more reasons you give, the more you invite negotiation. Each reason is a door they can push.
One sentence: 'I can't this weekend.' Warmth optional, explanation unnecessary.
If they push, repeat it in fewer words. 'Yeah, I can't.' Don't add new reasons.
Offer an alternative only if you actually want to. A fake alternative is just a slower no.

codes.title: When you're losing someone
lines: Shorter answers, eyes drifting, phone checks, body angled away. Those are the signs.
Don't talk faster or louder. That's the instinct, and it makes it worse.
Either change the energy with a question about them, or end it cleanly: 'I'll let you get back to your friends. Good talking to you.'
A clean exit when someone is fading earns more aura than a rescue attempt that fails.

codes.title: Taking a roast
lines: The worst response to being roasted is defending yourself. It tells the room it landed.
Laugh first. Agree and exaggerate, or land one back that's lighter than theirs.
Never punch harder than you got hit. You want the room laughing with both of you.
If it actually hurt, deal with it later, one on one. Not in front of the group.

codes.title: Land the ending
lines: Stories die in the last ten percent. 'So yeah… anyway… that's it' throws away everything before it.
Know your last line before you start. It should be a punchline, a point, or a question back.
Say it at the same volume as your first line, then stop.
Trailing off asks the listener to rescue you. Ending cleanly hands them the next turn.

codes.title: Eye contact under pressure
lines: You don't need to stare. Look at them at the start and end of every sentence.
When you're thinking, it's fine to look away. Look back when you deliver the point.
On camera, the lens is their eyes. Glancing at your own face reads as nerves.
The moment people look down is usually the moment they say the important thing. Flip that.

codes.title: Money conversations
lines: Money gets awkward because people hint instead of asking. Hints feel safe and get ignored.
Be specific and early: 'I only had the salad, I'll put in thirty.' Not after the bill lands.
When someone owes you, ask once, directly, with a date: 'Can you send the two hundred by Friday?'
You can be generous by choice. Being vague is how you end up paying for other people.
